Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending in the year to June 2026. Capital spending is money put into long-lived assets, such as data centers. Even so, Microsoft had cash left over.

Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0%, a chip-stock fund (SMH) 10.6% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Microsoft fell 2.8%, less than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%.

Source: Microsoft's cash-flow statements, fiscal years ending June 30. "Left over" is cash brought in minus capital spending, buybacks and dividends. A negative "borrowed" means it repaid more debt than it took on.

Microsoft's capital spending reached $116 billion in its last fiscal year, up from $65 billion. It still paid shareholders nearly $49 billion. It also paid down $3 billion of debt. Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds.

Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders' cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending and still paid its shareholders nearly $49 billion. If you want your savings to pay you an income, that kind of cash is what to look for. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

Can Microsoft Spend More Next Year?

Yes, about $39 billion more from its own cash.

Analysts expect sales of $396 billion in the year to June 2027, or fiscal 2027. Microsoft turns about 57 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. On those sales, that is about $224 billion.

Key Takeaways

Snowflake fell 12% in the past week as the AI trade sold off, and the company itself had no bad news.

RBC's Matthew Hedberg put Snowflake among the few software companies he sees with real AI acceleration, along with Cloudflare and CrowdStrike.

UBS and BofA cut their price targets but kept their Buy ratings, and Oppenheimer and Morgan Stanley expect a product revenue beat when Snowflake reports on Dec. 2.

The stock got cheaper while earnings estimates rose, so it looks like a buy before the report, as long as product gross margin holds at 74%.

Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE) has dropped 12% in the past week, and the company didn't report anything to cause it. The whole AI trade sold off, led by the chipmakers, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 10%. Anthropic's IPO was priced bigger than planned, but it didn't turn things around on Thursday.

That's a rough week for a stock one analyst had just put in AI's top tier. On Nov. 17, RBC Capital Markets software analyst Matthew Hedberg talked with Dan Nathan on the RiskReversal Pod about software stocks and the market's AI worries. He said he has "seen clear AI leadership from five or six names that I cover where there's real acceleration." Snowflake made his list, along with Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ), Cloudflare (NET:NYSE), CrowdStrike (CRWD:NASDAQ) and Palo Alto.

Nobody downgraded it

Snowflake's only news this week came from analysts, and all of them kept their Buy ratings. UBS cut its target to $450 from $500 on Nov. 18. BofA cut its target to $400 from $470 on Nov. 20 and said demand trends were still strong. Also on Nov. 18, Oppenheimer and Morgan Stanley said Snowflake should beat its fiscal third-quarter product revenue guidance.

Investors are nervous because of Datadog, which also bills by usage. Its third-quarter revenue grew 35% to $1.20 billion. Then it guided to $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion for the fourth quarter, about flat with the third quarter, after its largest customer, an AI company, cut back its usage. Datadog's stock is down 15% in the past week too. But that was one customer, and no single Snowflake customer makes up even 10% of revenue.

What Dec. 2 has to show

Snowflake reports after the close on Dec. 2. It has guided to product revenue of $1.588 billion to $1.593 billion, up 37% to 38%. Goldman Sachs Just Dropped 14% in a Week. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@JayLazarin from Getty Images Signature via Canva, @Vertigo3d from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Goldman Sachs stock fell 14% in the past week, more than the S&P 500 and Morgan Stanley, as an AI-led selloff spread to bank stocks.

Nearly half of the drop came Friday. That morning, SpaceX's lenders reportedly balked at Elon Musk's plans for the chips behind their loans, and the same day Goldman and Apollo priced about $44 billion of notes to fund SpaceX's GPUs.

Goldman's own news was good, including about $113 million in fees from Anthropic's IPO. Even so, the stock still trades well above its five-year average multiple of tangible book.

The stock is a hold: its price still assumes near-20% returns, and fourth-quarter results in mid-January are the next test.

Goldman Sachs (GS:NYSE) stock is down 14% in the past week, a bigger drop than the S&P 500's 9% or the Nasdaq 100's 10%. Most of the damage came Friday, the same day Goldman and Apollo Global Management (APO:NYSE) priced about $44 billion of notes to buy AI chips for SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ).

Morgan Stanley (MS:NYSE) fell 13% over the same stretch, so some of this is a broad selloff in bank stocks. But Goldman fell further. My read: investors were selling the bank most tied to financing the AI buildout.

TIKR tracks 26 analysts on Goldman Sachs. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Goldman Sachs, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Goldman Sachs' Analyst Ratings

The SpaceX deal priced at a bad moment

On Friday morning, a Financial Times report said lenders on SpaceX's chip-backed debt had tried to stop Elon Musk from launching that collateral into orbit. SpaceX stock fell below its IPO price. Later that morning, Apollo and Goldman announced they had priced about $44 billion of senior and subordinated notes to fund GPUs and related equipment for SpaceX.

Not ideal timing.

Goldman had been selling pieces of SpaceX's GPU debt since early November. That included an $8.3 billion senior-secured loan it reportedly led, which was being sold on to other banks. Apollo's results rest on lending. CEO Marc Rowan said its model "starts with originating increasing amounts of good assets," and origination hit a record $114 billion in the third quarter. If lenders keep balking at Musk's plans, investors will want to know how much of the SpaceX paper each firm kept on its own books.

The deal flow is still there

What's odd is how good Goldman's own week looked. Goldman and Morgan Stanley led Anthropic's IPO, and by Fortune's count each bank earned about $113 million in fees. That's more than either made on SpaceX's IPO.

Alibaba Sinks 25% in a Month as Chip Curbs Threaten Its 20 GW Plan: Eddie Wu Warns of "Downward Revision" ©@Kaspars Grinvalds via Canva; @Karola G from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Alibaba fell 25% in a month to a 52-week low as Washington moved to block Chinese companies from Nvidia chips rented abroad.

Nvidia can't sell its top chips in China anyway, so the curbs hurt Alibaba's cloud far more.

External cloud recurring revenue grew 67% last quarter, but CEO Eddie Wu said Alibaba's 20 GW data-center target may be revised down.

The stock looks cheap, but estimates have barely moved, so buying in small pieces makes sense.

Alibaba (BABA:NYSE) stock is down 25% in the past month and hit a 52-week low on Nov. 20. The Nasdaq 100 fell 15% over the same stretch. The rest came from Washington, which is moving to cut Chinese companies off from the Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips they rent abroad.

Washington went after the chips Alibaba rents

On Nov. 9, the Financial Times reported that Alibaba is the largest client of Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of Nvidia's scandal. On Nov. 11, The Information reported Commerce was close to finalizing a new rule. It would bar Chinese companies from advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, Singapore included. Alibaba fell 7% the next day. The rule took effect Nov. 19, giving data centers already serving Chinese companies 90 days to get licenses.

Nvidia is down 42% over the month, and Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 amid the scandal. But its top chips are already barred from China, so it loses little from the curbs.

The cloud delivered, but the build may shrink

The Nov. 19 report showed real demand: external cloud customers' recurring revenue rose 67%. But on the call, Wu said shifting compute policies "may lead to a downward revision of that long-term 20 GW target," with "a certain impact" on capex. He guided cloud growth to 30% to 45% in the fiscal year starting April 2027.

After the report, Barclays cut its target to $155 from $200, citing the lower compute ambition. Mizuho raised its to $205 from $200.

Key Takeaways

Palantir stock fell 25% in the past month, even though third-quarter revenue grew 96% and the company raised its full-year guidance.

Slower bookings, worries about the Pentagon budget under a Democratic Congress, and Anthropic's IPO gave investors reasons to pay less, while Datadog fell even further in the same AI software selloff.

Palantir's forward P/E is far below its five-year average, and analysts keep raising their earnings estimates.

The stock looks worth buying in pieces, and the next test is Palantir's first 2027 guidance in early February against a $13.1 billion revenue consensus.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) just grew revenue 96% in a quarter, and its stock is down 25% in the past month anyway.

The Nasdaq 100 fell about 15% over the same stretch, and Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) fell even further after a strong quarter. Then, Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) began trading on Nov. 19, a new yardstick for what AI growth is worth.

TIKR tracks 34 analysts on Palantir. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Palantir, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Palantir's Analyst Ratings

A soft spot in a huge quarter

Third-quarter revenue rose 96% to $2.313 billion, U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, and management raised its full-year revenue guidance to 8.530-8.534 billion.

The soft spot was new business. Total contract value grew just 6% to $2.918 billion, after 49% growth in the second quarter, and U.S. commercial remaining deal value rose only 4% from June. Management tied it to Sovereign AI customers signing shorter deals, and the stock fell the day after the report.

Analysts expect revenue growth to slow from about 91% this year to 53% in 2027:

Palantir Technologies (PLTR): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)
Washington is a smaller risk than it looks

On Nov. 5, with no news of its own, Palantir fell 9.73% with AI and defense stocks after reports that the Democrats' sweep of Congress had raised fears of a smaller Pentagon budget and slower AI data-center spending. CEO Alex Karp is already courting the new majority, telling Politico that "all of our products are essentially progressive."

A tighter budget could slow U.S. government revenue, which grew 96% to $953 million in the third quarter. But U.S. commercial revenue passed it for the first time that quarter, and is growing faster. Palantir now has a second engine at least as big as the first.
